structure.rationale: The request asked for one small web application rather than an ecosystem tour, so the ten chapters follow the order in which a single Task Tracker API actually grows: project first, then one endpoint, then a full resource, then the layering that keeps it from rotting, then input validation, persistence, configuration, tests, a login gate, and finally packaging it to run outside the IDE. Each chapter adds exactly one capability to the same running project, so nothing is explained before the reader has felt the need for it. Deferred on purpose, per the request: microservices, reactive, messaging, Kubernetes, cloud, OAuth and JWT.
structure.audience: Working programmers who know some Java but have never built a Spring application.

claims.text: Spring Boot 4.1.0 was published on 10 June 2026 and is the current recommended baseline for new projects.
Spring Boot 4.0 requires Java 17 or later.
Spring Boot minor versions ship roughly every six months and each carries about 12 months of open-source support, so a new project should start on the newest minor.

Spring is the underlying framework (dependency injection, MVC, data access); Spring Boot is a layer on top that auto-configures sensible defaults, bundles an embedded server, and lets an app run as a plain JAR with a main method.
start.spring.io (Spring Initializr) generates the project skeleton — build file, main class, and test class — from a chosen build tool, language, Boot version and dependency list.
In Spring Boot 4 the web starter is spring-boot-starter-webmvc; the old spring-boot-starter-web name is deprecated in favour of it.
@SpringBootApplication on the main class combines configuration, auto-configuration and component scanning; SpringApplication.run starts the context and the embedded server.

snippets.note: Boot 4.1 Maven skeleton; starter renamed from spring-boot-starter-web.
The entire bootstrap; Initializr generates exactly this.

pitfalls: Copying a pre-4.0 tutorial's spring-boot-starter-web into a Boot 4 build: it is the deprecated name, and tutorials rarely say which Boot version they targeted.
Assuming the newest Java release is required — Boot 4 needs only Java 17, and an LTS release is the safer choice.

claims.text: When spring-webmvc is on the classpath, Spring Boot auto-configures a DispatcherServlet and an embedded server, and component scanning discovers the application's controllers.
@RestController combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, so a handler's return value becomes the response body instead of a view name.
@GetMapping maps an HTTP GET to a handler method; a returned String becomes a text/plain body and a returned object is serialized to JSON.
Spring Boot 4 uses Jackson 3 as its preferred JSON library, whose group id moved from com.fasterxml.jackson to tools.jackson; Jackson 2 support ships deprecated.
The embedded server listens on port 8080 by default.

snippets.note: A String body vs. a record serialized to JSON by Jackson.

pitfalls: Using @Controller instead of @RestController and getting a 404 as Spring tries to resolve the returned string as a view name.
Placing the controller outside the main class's package, where component scanning never reaches it.

claims.text: @PathVariable binds a URI template segment to a method parameter; @RequestParam binds a query-string parameter and can carry a default.
@RequestBody deserializes the request body into an object; @PostMapping, @PutMapping and @DeleteMapping map the corresponding HTTP methods.
ResponseEntity lets a handler set the status code and headers explicitly — 201 Created with a Location header for a successful POST, 204 No Content for a successful DELETE.
Returning a plain object implies 200 OK; returning void implies 200 unless a status is declared, so @ResponseStatus or ResponseEntity is needed for anything else.
Spring Boot 4.1 auto-configures API versioning for Spring MVC via spring.mvc.apiversion.* properties.

snippets.note: The Task Tracker resource; status codes set explicitly.

pitfalls: Returning 200 for a creation instead of 201 with a Location header.
Letting a missing task fall through as an empty 200 body rather than a 404.
Accepting the full entity as the request body, which lets a client set the id.

claims.text: Spring's dependency injection wires collaborators; constructor injection is the recommended style because it makes dependencies explicit and the object final and testable.
A class with a single constructor needs no @Autowired annotation — Spring uses that constructor automatically.
@Service and @Repository are @Component stereotypes picked up by component scanning; @Repository additionally translates persistence exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy.

Spring Boot 4 splits the formerly monolithic spring-boot-autoconfigure module into many fine-grained modules, so auto-configuration now arrives with the specific starter rather than one catch-all jar.

snippets.note: Constructor injection; the controller holds none of this logic.

pitfalls: Field injection with @Autowired, which hides dependencies and blocks constructing the class in a plain unit test.
Business rules drifting into the controller, so they can only be tested through HTTP.

claims.text: Spring Boot 4 builds on Jakarta Validation 3.1; the validation starter is spring-boot-starter-validation.
@Valid on a @RequestBody parameter triggers Jakarta Bean Validation before the handler body runs.
A failed @Valid on a request body raises MethodArgumentNotValidException, whose BindingResult carries one FieldError per violated constraint.
@RestControllerAdvice registers @ExceptionHandler methods globally across controllers, keeping error mapping in one place.
ProblemDetail is Spring's RFC 7807 problem-details representation and is the idiomatic error body for a REST API.
Common Jakarta constraints include @NotBlank (non-null and not only whitespace), @Size (length bounds) and @NotNull.

snippets.note: Constraints on the request record, not the entity.
One advice class turns exceptions into RFC 7807 bodies.

pitfalls: Adding constraint annotations but forgetting @Valid, so nothing is ever checked.
Returning a raw stack trace or the framework's default error body, which leaks internals and tells the client nothing actionable.

claims.text: JPA maps Java classes to relational tables; Hibernate is the implementation Spring Boot uses by default.
The persistence starter is spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, with a companion test starter spring-boot-starter-data-jpa-test in Boot 4's per-technology test-starter scheme.
An entity is a class annotated @Entity with an @Id field; @GeneratedValue lets the database assign the key.
Extending JpaRepository<T, ID> gives save, findById, findAll, deleteById and more with no implementation written — Spring Data generates the proxy at runtime.
Spring Data derives queries from method names, so findByDoneTrue() becomes a where clause without any SQL.
H2 is an in-memory database convenient for development; switching to PostgreSQL is a dependency and property change, not a code change.
Spring Boot 4.1 adds lazy datasource connections via spring.datasource.connection-fetch=lazy.
Apache Derby support is deprecated as of Spring Boot 4.1, following Derby's retirement.

snippets.note: JPA requires a no-arg constructor, which is why an entity is not a record.
Derived queries; no implementation class exists.

pitfalls: Trying to make an entity a Java record — JPA needs a no-arg constructor and mutable fields.
Leaving spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update switched on in production, letting the app rewrite the schema.
Returning entities straight from controllers, which couples the JSON contract to the table.

claims.text: Spring Boot reads application.properties or application.yml from src/main/resources; the two formats are interchangeable.
Configuration is resolved from an ordered set of property sources, where command-line arguments and environment variables override the packaged files.
A property such as spring.datasource.url can be supplied as the environment variable SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL using relaxed binding.
Profiles let environment-specific files such as application-prod.yml layer over the defaults, activated with spring.profiles.active.
@ConfigurationProperties binds a group of properties to a typed object, which is checked at startup rather than scattered through @Value annotations.
Spring Boot 4.1 lets configuration-file imports declare their encoding.

snippets.code:
spring:
  application:
    name: task-tracker
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:h2:mem:tasks
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: update

tasks:
  max-per-user: 100

snippets.note: Typed binding; a record works here because nothing needs to mutate it.

pitfalls: Committing production credentials to application.yml instead of supplying them as environment variables.
Assuming a profile file replaces the base file — it layers on top, and unset keys keep their defaults.

claims.text: A service with constructor-injected collaborators can be unit tested with plain JUnit and a mock, with no Spring context started.
@WebMvcTest loads only the web layer for a controller test, so it starts far faster than a full application context.
@SpringBootTest starts the whole application context and is the integration-test entry point.

Spring Boot 4 adds support for RestTestClient: with a regular @SpringBootTest, or when @AutoConfigureMockMvc is used, a RestTestClient can be autowired that operates on the underlying MockMvc instance.
Boot 4's modularization gives each technology a companion test starter following the pattern spring-boot-starter-<technology>-test.
Tests run with ./mvnw test under Maven or ./gradlew test under Gradle.

snippets.note: No Spring context — this is why constructor injection was worth it.
Web slice only; the service is replaced by a test double.

pitfalls: Reaching for @SpringBootTest for everything, which turns a fast suite into a slow one.
Testing only the happy path, when the validation and 404 branches are where the bugs live.

claims.text: Spring Boot 4 ships Spring Security 7.0; Spring Boot 4.1 ships Spring Security 7.1.0.
Adding the Spring Security starter secures every endpoint by default — an unauthenticated request gets 401 before any controller runs.
Security is configured by declaring a SecurityFilterChain bean, the recommended style since Spring Security 5.4.
In Spring Security 7 the Lambda DSL is required: the older chained style using .and() has been removed.
authorizeRequests() was removed in Spring Security 7; authorizeHttpRequests() replaces it and is backed by AuthorizationManager and AuthorizationFilter rather than FilterSecurityInterceptor.
Because the new authorization model also checks dispatch types including error dispatches, an unauthenticated /error render can return 401 after migrating.
Customizer.withDefaults() enables a feature with Spring Security's defaults and is shorthand for the empty lambda it -> {}.
HTTP Basic sends credentials on every request and is only acceptable over HTTPS; it suits a first example, not a public production API.
Passwords are stored as hashes; BCryptPasswordEncoder is the common default, and an InMemoryUserDetailsManager holds demo users without a database.
CSRF protection defends browser session flows; it is commonly disabled for a stateless token or Basic API, which is a deliberate trade-off rather than a default to ignore.
Spring Boot 4.1 adds HTTP client SSRF mitigation via InetAddressFilter.

snippets.note: Spring Security 7 style: Lambda DSL, authorizeHttpRequests, no .and().

pitfalls: Copying a pre-7.0 config that uses authorizeRequests() or .and() — neither compiles against Spring Security 7.
Storing plaintext passwords, or calling encode() on an already-encoded value.
Disabling CSRF reflexively on an app that does use browser sessions and forms.

claims.text: Spring Boot uses SLF4J with Logback by default; a logger is obtained per class and levels are set with logging.level.* properties.
Spring Boot 4.1 adds file rotation support for Log4j with four strategies: size, time, size-and-time, and cron.
./mvnw package builds an executable fat JAR containing the application, its dependencies and the embedded server, runnable with java -jar.
The Maven and Gradle plugins can build an OCI container image directly with spring-boot:build-image, using Cloud Native Buildpacks and requiring no hand-written Dockerfile.
The layertools jar mode was removed in Spring Boot 4.1 and replaced by the tools jar mode.
Spring Boot 4.1 expands the /actuator/info ProcessInfo section with six new fields.

snippets.code:
./mvnw package
java -jar target/task-tracker-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar

# container image, no Dockerfile required
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image
snippets.note: The fat JAR is the deployable unit; buildpacks wrap it in an image.

snippets.code:
private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(TaskService.class);

log.info("Completed task {}", id);   // placeholder, never string concatenation
snippets.note: Parameterized logging avoids building the string when the level is off.

pitfalls: Building the plain JAR rather than the repackaged one and hitting 'no main manifest attribute'.
Logging with string concatenation, which pays the formatting cost even when the level is disabled.
Following a Boot 3 tutorial that uses the removed layertools jar mode.
